title: Weather Wendy's Forecast
text:
Good morning! This is Weather Wendy with your forecast for Maple Town.

Today will start out sunny and {adjective}. Around lunchtime, a light breeze will blow in from the lake. It will smell a little bit like {food}.

This afternoon, look out for a gentle shower of {plural noun}. They will fall softly, so you may want to carry a {noun} instead of an umbrella. Tonight the clouds will turn {color} and start {verb ending in ing}. Experts say this is perfectly normal for a Tuesday.

Tomorrow, the temperature will reach {number} degrees. Please wear sunscreen, a hat, and your most {adjective} sneakers. The wind will blow {adverb} all day. This has been Weather Wendy. Remember, if the sky starts to {verb}, just go inside and have a snack!

title: Breaking News from Puddle Lane
text:
This is Max Miller with breaking news from Puddle Lane.

At nine o'clock this morning, a small {adjective} cloud floated over Lincoln School and began raining {plural noun}. Students watched {adverb} from the classroom windows.

"I have never seen anything like it," said Principal Gray. "It was very {adjective}. We had to skip recess and {verb} instead."

The cloud then moved to the park, where it rained on a man {verb ending in ing} with his dog. The man said it felt like being tickled by a {noun}.

Weather experts say the cloud is shaped like a {animal} and is now heading toward the library. Neighbors are asked to keep their windows closed and their {plural noun} indoors.

We will keep you updated. Back to you, {name}!

title: My Weather Journal for Science
text:
Our teacher, Mr. Reed, asked us to write down the weather every day this week. Here is my weather journal.

Monday: Sunny and warm. A cloud shaped like a {noun} floated over my house all day.
Tuesday: Very windy. The wind blew my hat off and carried it {adverb} all the way to the {place}.
Wednesday: Foggy. The fog was so thick that I said good morning to a {noun}.
Thursday: It rained for {number} hours. The puddles were deep enough to {verb} in.
Friday: A rainbow came out after lunch. It had red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple, and {color}.

I measured the rain with a cup. On Thursday it filled up with water and three {plural noun}. Mr. Reed says that is very {adjective} and I should write a report about it.

Next week I will try to catch a snowflake and keep it in the freezer next to the {plural noun}.

title: Snowman Instructions from a Snow Expert
text:
When it snows, everyone wants to build a snowman. Here is how to make the best one on your street.

Step 1: Put on your boots, your mittens, and your {adjective} scarf.
Step 2: Roll a big ball of snow for the bottom. Keep rolling until it is as big as a {noun}.
Step 3: Make a middle-sized ball for his tummy and a little one on top for his face. Stack them {adverb}.
Step 4: Give your snowman a face. Use two {plural noun} for the eyes and a carrot for the nose.
Step 5: Add sticks for arms. Some people also give their snowman a {noun} to hold.
Step 6: Name your snowman. Ours is named {silly word}.

When you are done, stand back and say hello. If your snowman starts to {verb}, that means you did a great job. Last winter, ours {past tense verb} all the way to the mailbox and back. Then go inside and drink hot cocoa with {plural noun} on top.

title: Windy Day Rules at School
text:
Good morning, students! This is Principal Park with an important announcement. The weather report says today will be the windiest day of the year.

Please follow these windy day rules:
1. Hold on to your homework {adverb}. Yesterday, the spelling tests blew all the way to the {noun}.
2. Do not fly kites at lunch. Last time, a kite pulled Mr. Bell's {noun} right off the table.
3. If your hair starts to look {adjective}, that is okay. Everyone's hair will look that way today.
4. Keep your hats in your backpacks. We do not want any more hats stuck on the flagpole next to the {plural noun}.
5. If you see a flying {noun}, please do not chase it. Tell a teacher, and a teacher will {verb} until it lands.

Recess will be indoors today. We will play board games, read books, and do the {animal} dance in the gym. Thank you for {verb ending in ing} so nicely. Have a {adjective} day!

title: A Letter to Mr. Cloud
text:
Dear Mr. Cloud,

My name is Lily. I am seven years old, and I live in the yellow house on Oak Street. You float over my house almost every day.

I have a few questions for you. Why are you so {adjective} on Mondays? Do you ever get tired of {verb ending in ing}? What do you eat for breakfast? My grandpa says clouds eat {plural noun}, but I think he is joking.

I also have a favor to ask. My birthday party is on Saturday. Could you please rain {plural noun} instead of water? That would be so {adjective}. My friends would love it. If you say yes, I will {verb} {adverb} for you and draw you a picture of a {noun}.

Your friend on the ground,
Lily

P.S. Please tell the rainbow I like its {color} stripe the best.

title: Grandma Sky's Rainbow Recipe
text:
Have you ever wondered how a rainbow is made? Here is the secret recipe, straight from Grandma Sky's kitchen.

You will need:
1 big cloud
2 cups of sunshine
A bucket of rain
A pinch of glitter
A {adjective} spoon

First, put the cloud in a large bowl. Pour in the rain and stir it {adverb} until it starts to {verb}. Then add the sunshine one cup at a time.

Next, sprinkle in the glitter and a handful of {plural noun}. Grandma Sky says this is what makes the colors so {adjective}. If you want an extra stripe, add a little bit of {food}.

Bake the rainbow in the sky for {number} minutes. When it is done, it should stretch from the school all the way to the {noun}. Serve it after a rainy afternoon, and do not forget to shout "{exclamation}!"

title: Greetings from Breezy Hills
text:
Dear Aunt Rose,

Greetings from Breezy Hills, the windiest town in the whole country! We are staying here for {number} days.

The wind here never stops. This morning it blew my pancakes right off my plate and onto a {noun}. Mom had to hold on to her {adjective} sunglasses all through breakfast.

Everybody in town flies kites. Our neighbor has a kite shaped like a {animal} that is as big as a bus. Dad bought me a kite too. It flew {adverb} and got stuck on a {noun} for an hour.

Yesterday we went to the Wind Museum. They have a jar of wind from long ago. It smells like {plural noun}. The museum guide told us to {verb} when he opened it. Tomorrow we will see the Breezy Hills Parade, where everyone goes {verb ending in ing} down Main Street.

Love,
Ben

title: Dr. Riley's Weather Facts
text:
Hi! I am Dr. Riley, junior weather scientist. Here are some fun facts about weather that I learned this year.

Fact 1: Snowflakes have six sides. No two snowflakes look the same, but some look a little bit like {plural noun}.
Fact 2: Thunder is the sound clouds make when they try to {verb}.
Fact 3: Hail is little balls of ice. In my town, the hail is soft and about the size of a {noun}.
Fact 4: Fog is a cloud that got sleepy and decided to {verb} on the ground.
Fact 5: The hottest day ever in my backyard was {number} degrees. My popsicle melted {adverb} and dripped on my {body part}.
Fact 6: When it rains while the sun is out, a {adjective} rainbow appears. If you look closely, you can see a {animal} {verb ending in ing} on it.

I want to be a real weather scientist when I grow up. I will wear a {adjective} lab coat and drive a truck full of {plural noun}.

title: The Town Weather Order Form
text:
Thank you for calling the Town Weather Office! To order your weather, please fill out this form and drop it in the {adjective} box outside City Hall.

Name: Jada, age 7
Weather needed for: Saturday, my soccer game
What kind of sky would you like? A blue sky with {number} fluffy clouds. Please make one of the clouds look like a {noun}.
How warm should it be? Warm enough to {verb} outside, but not so hot that my {food} melts.
Would you like wind? Yes, please. Just a little bit, so our team flag can wave {adverb}.

Anything else? If it has to rain, please make it rain {plural noun}. Our coach says that would be very {adjective}. Also, please send a rainbow right after the game. My whole team will be {verb ending in ing} on the field when it shows up.

Thank you! I will pay you with a hug and two {plural noun}.
